section.title: Lead Me in Your Righteousness
section.sectionRationale: A morning prayer for guidance, built on the contrast between a God who cannot dwell with evil and the abundant loving devotion that opens His house to those who take refuge in Him.
section.thesis: Because God delights in righteousness and has no pleasure in wickedness, David lays his morning plea before God's holy temple by His abundant loving devotion, asking to be led safely past his enemies while all who take refuge in the LORD rejoice under His favor.
section.frameNote: Five movements: the morning plea (vv1-3), God's holiness contrasted with the wicked (vv4-6), David's own approach by God's loving devotion (vv7-8), the deceit of the enemies (vv9-10), and the joy of those who take refuge in the LORD (vv11-12).

units.label: A morning plea
units.note: at daybreak I lay my plea before You

verses.text: Give ear to my words, O LORD; consider my groaning.
Attend to the sound of my cry, my King and my God, for to You I pray.
In the morning, O LORD, You hear my voice; at daybreak I lay my plea before You and wait in expectation.

units.label: God's holiness and the wicked
units.note: no evil can dwell with You

verses.text: For You are not a God who delights in wickedness; no evil can dwell with You.
The boastful cannot stand in Your presence; You hate all workers of iniquity.
You destroy those who tell lies; the LORD abhors the man of bloodshed and deceit.

units.label: Lead me by Your loving devotion
units.note: make straight Your way before me

verses.text: But I will enter Your house by the abundance of Your {{chesed|loving devotion}}; in reverence I will bow down toward Your holy temple.
Lead me, O LORD, in Your righteousness because of my enemies; make straight Your way before me.
For not a word they speak can be trusted; destruction lies within them. Their throats are open graves; their tongues practice deceit.
Declare them guilty, O God; let them fall by their own devices. Drive them out for their many transgressions, for they have rebelled against You.

units.label: Joy for those who take refuge

verses.text: But let all who take refuge in You rejoice; let them ever shout for joy. May You shelter them, that those who love Your name may rejoice in You.
For surely You, O LORD, bless the righteous; You surround them with the shield of Your favor.

chesed.gloss: Steadfast love, loyal covenant devotion, God's committed kindness to His people. David's confidence to enter God's house at all rests entirely on the abundance of this loving devotion, not on his own worthiness, a theme that runs through the whole Psalter.

basic.context: Psalm 5 is a morning prayer for guidance, set against enemies whose words cannot be trusted. David appeals first to God's own holy character, a God who cannot delight in wickedness, and then to God's abundant loving devotion as the only ground on which he can approach the holy temple at all.
basic.hermeneutics: This psalm is prayed by a righteous sufferer surrounded by liars and slanderers, and it teaches that approaching God is never a matter of personal merit but always of His abundant loving devotion; the call for God to declare the wicked guilty is an appeal to divine justice, not private revenge.
basic.originalLanguages: David enters God's house only 'by the abundance of Your chesed,' steadfast covenant love, not by his own righteousness. The image of enemies whose throat is an open grave pictures speech that swallows the innocent, a vivid ancient Near Eastern figure for deadly deceit.
basic.typology: David's approach to God's house solely on the basis of God's loving devotion anticipates the gospel pattern completed in Christ, who is Himself the temple and the mercy by which sinners now enter God's presence, Hebrews 10:19-22.
basic.christ: Jesus is the one true righteous sufferer surrounded by deceitful accusers whose words could not be trusted, Mark 14:56, and He is also the one through whom every believer now enters God's presence, not by their own merit but by His mediating loving devotion.
basic.god: God is both utterly holy, unable to delight in wickedness or let evil dwell with Him, and abundantly loving, opening His house to sinners who come by His mercy rather than their own standing, a tension the whole psalm holds together without resolving it into either bare severity or soft sentiment.
basic.crossReferences: Romans 3:13 quotes this psalm's picture of throats as open graves to describe universal human sinfulness. Hebrews 10:19-22 describes entering God's presence by a new and living way opened in Christ. Psalm 91:4 echoes the image of God as a shield.
basic.oneStory: Psalm 5 teaches that no one enters God's presence by their own righteousness but only by His abundant loving devotion, a truth the whole Bible drives toward and fulfills in Jesus Christ, who opens the way into the true temple for all who take refuge in Him.

context.literary:
The psalm is built on a hinge word. Verses 4 to 6 speak of God in the third person and in negatives: not a God who delights in wickedness, evil cannot dwell, the boastful cannot stand. Then verse 7 turns on 'But I,' and the prayer moves from what God is not able to tolerate to how a person may nevertheless come near. Verse 11 opens with a second 'But,' this time for the whole company of the faithful. So the psalm has a rhythm of threat, turn, threat, turn, and each turn is a door left open by God's own generosity.

The opening cluster of verses 1 to 3 climbs in three steps. David asks God to hear his words, then his groaning, then the bare sound of his cry. It is as though speech is failing and prayer is falling back on noise. The verbs of the morning scene are unusually physical: he lays out his plea and then keeps watch, like a sentry, for the answer.

The enemies of verses 9 and 10 are drawn as a body taken apart: a mouth with no truth in it, an inward part full of ruin, a throat that is a tomb, a tongue that smooths and flatters. The righteous, by contrast, are described by what surrounds and covers them, a shelter and a shield, verses 11 and 12. Wickedness is all speech and appetite; the righteous are held.

Notice too the movement of space. David enters a house, bows toward a temple, asks for a straight road, and ends with a shield that circles a whole people. The psalm travels from the doorway to the road to the community, and its final verse widens the private 'I' of verse 1 into the many who love God's name.
context.historical:
The heading assigns the psalm to David and directs it to the choirmaster, with an instrument term the BSB renders as flutes. That places it in the worship life of Israel from early on, and the setting it describes is the daily rhythm of the sanctuary. Every morning a lamb was offered at the altar, Exodus 29:38-42, and the offering was set out in order, layer upon layer of wood and flesh and flour. David's verb for laying out his plea is the same kind of word, the language of arranging something on an altar. His prayer is meant to rise with the morning sacrifice.

Morning also had a legal weight in Israel. Kings were told to 'administer justice every morning,' Jeremiah 21:12, and God Himself 'applies His justice morning by morning,' Zephaniah 3:5. A person with false accusers would wait for dawn as the hour when a case could be heard. David's 'wait in expectation' is the posture of a litigant at the gate, and the psalm's harsh language about liars and men of bloodshed suits the atmosphere of a court where slander could cost a life.

The 'house' and 'holy temple' of verse 7 raise an obvious question, since Solomon's temple was built after David. But the sanctuary at Shiloh was already called the temple of the LORD, 1 Samuel 1:9 and 3:3, and David himself 'went into the house of the LORD and worshiped,' 2 Samuel 12:20. The vocabulary of a temple existed long before the stone building.

The psalm does not name David's enemies. Their description, boastful, bloodthirsty, deceitful, fits a court or a household where reputations were destroyed by whispers. The first hearers would have taken the psalm as a template for any honest person living among people who lie for advantage.
context.canonical:
Psalms 3 to 5 read as a small sequence about days and nights. Psalm 3 wakes with the LORD's sustaining, 'I lie down and sleep; I wake again,' verse 5, Psalm 4 lies down at night in peace, and Psalm 5 rises at daybreak. Together they teach a person to shut and open the day in prayer. Jesus follows exactly this habit when He goes out 'early in the morning, while it was still dark,' to pray in a solitary place, Mark 1:35.

The psalm also carries forward the two-ways theme that opens the Psalter. Psalm 1 divides the righteous from the wicked, and Psalm 2 ends with 'Blessed are all who take refuge in Him,' verse 12. Psalm 5:11 picks up that very word, refuge, and gives it its first sustained use in the prayers of David. The one who takes refuge is the one who is blessed and shielded.

Its sharpest New Testament use is in Romans 3. Paul strings together a chain of Psalm quotations to show that Jew and Gentile alike are under sin, and the line 'Their throats are open graves; their tongues practice deceit,' Romans 3:13, comes from this psalm, followed by a line from Psalm 140:3 about the venom of vipers. In David's mouth the words describe his enemies. In Paul's they describe every human being, so that 'every mouth may be silenced,' Romans 3:19.

The question of who may come into God's house also echoes through Psalm 15, 'who may abide in Your tent,' and Psalm 24, 'who may ascend the hill of the LORD,' verses 3 and 4. Psalm 5 gives the answer that those psalms leave hanging: a person comes not by his own qualifications but by the abundance of God's loving devotion.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
David wrote for a worshipper who has to face the day with people who lie, and he wanted Israel to see that the first move in such a day is not a plan but an audience. The prayer is arranged so that the reader learns an order of approach: speak to the King, wait for Him, remember who He is, come in by His mercy, ask for a road, and then, and only then, name the trouble. Nearly half of the psalm is spent on God's character before the enemies are described in detail.

David also meant to draw a line through the crowd. There are two kinds of people in this psalm, those whose speech is smooth and empty and those who take refuge, and there is no third group standing safely in the middle. The psalm asks the singer which group he belongs to, and it teaches him that the answer is settled by where he runs for shelter, not by how well he speaks.

The closing verses turn the private prayer into a song for a congregation. A choirmaster was to lead the psalm, so the many were meant to learn what the one had learned: that the LORD blesses the righteous and surrounds them with favor. Those who sang it were to leave with joy, not merely with a grievance against their enemies.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm records what David believed and prayed in a specific season of slander. It does not command anyone to hold that every opponent is a limb of the wicked, or to pray for their downfall at breakfast. Verse 5 says God hates all workers of iniquity, and that sentence describes how God regards settled, boastful evil. It is not an instruction to hate people.

What the text does prescribe by example is a pattern. Bring your words, and even your groans, to God early. Wait for Him, and do not run ahead with your own answer. Ground your approach in His love, not your record, verse 7. Ask to be led, verse 8, rather than to be excused. Leave the verdict on the liars to God, verse 10.

The application has to pass through Romans 3:13. Once Paul has applied the open-grave line to every human being, a reader cannot use this psalm to sort the world into good people and bad people with himself on the good side. The psalm is safe to pray only with the humility of one who has come in by chesed. That is also why Jesus can tell us to love enemies, Matthew 5:44, without cancelling the psalm: we ask God to deal with evil and hope that our enemies are rescued from it too.

debates.question: Is the request 'declare them guilty, O God, let them fall by their own devices' a call for personal vengeance?

views.label: An appeal to God's justice, not personal revenge
views.case: David asks God, the righteous Judge, to act, and pictures the wicked falling into traps of their own making, language of just consequence rather than personal cruelty inflicted by David's own hand.

views.label: An imprecation to be read carefully in light of Christ's teaching to love enemies
views.case: Jesus commands prayer for persecutors, Matthew 5:44, so such prayers should be understood as longing for God's justice and the defeat of evil, offered alongside genuine hope for the enemy's repentance, rather than simple wishes for their ruin.

debates.bearing: Both readings affirm David is appealing to God's justice rather than acting as his own avenger, a pattern the New Testament commends, Romans 12:19.

debates.question: What does it mean that God 'hates all workers of iniquity'?

views.label: God hates the persons who persist in evil
views.case: The verse names the workers, not only the work, and Psalm 11:5 says of the LORD that 'His soul hates the lover of violence.' On this reading the Bible does not soften the point: God's opposition falls on people who stubbornly set themselves against Him.

views.label: God hates the evil and the settled opposition, not the sinner as a sinner
views.case: The word is set beside 'boastful' and 'those who tell lies,' verses 5 and 6, so the target is a stance of arrogant rebellion. Since God loves the world, John 3:16, and Christ died for us 'while we were still sinners,' Romans 5:8, His hatred of evil never cancels His willingness to save the evildoer.

views.label: Judicial language for a verdict already in view
views.case: Hate here can describe the settled position of a judge who will not acquit the guilty, which is why the same verse says such people cannot 'stand in Your presence.' The remedy is not to reword the verse but to see the way in that verse 7 offers.

debates.bearing: All three views agree that the psalm is not licence for personal hostility. It holds God's holiness and His mercy together, and the door in verse 7 shows that no one is barred from mercy by being a sinner.

debates.question: How can a psalm of David speak of a 'temple' and a 'house' if the temple came later?

views.label: David wrote it, using the language of the earlier sanctuary
views.case: The tent at Shiloh is called a temple in 1 Samuel 1:9 and 3:3, and David 'went into the house of the LORD' in 2 Samuel 12:20. The heading names David, and the vocabulary of a temple was already available to him.

views.label: The psalm was shaped or adapted for use in Solomon's temple
views.case: Some hold that the psalm reached its present form when it was used in the later temple liturgy, with the heading and wording fitted to that setting. The prayer would then be David's in origin and the community's in use.

debates.bearing: The teaching does not depend on the answer. Either way the psalm treats the sanctuary as the place where God has promised to meet His people, and asks how a sinner may enter it.

study.originalLanguages:
Several small words carry weight in this psalm. In verse 3 David says he will 'lay out' his plea. The Hebrew verb, arak, means to arrange things in order. It is used for setting out wood on an altar, Genesis 22:9, and for laying out a legal case before a judge, as Job hopes to do in Job 23:4. Both meanings suit the verse: a morning sacrifice and a prepared argument. The following verb, tsafah, is the word for keeping watch as a sentry does. David sets his prayer in order and then stands on the wall to see what God will do.

In verse 4, 'no evil can dwell with You' uses gur, to stay as a sojourner or guest. Psalm 15:1 asks 'who may abide in Your tent' with a form of this same verb. Evil is not allowed to lodge as a guest with God. The word for 'delights' in the same verse, chafets, is the language of pleasure and favor; God finds no enjoyment in wickedness. Verse 6 adds a strong word, 'abhors,' a word of moral disgust whose related noun gives the 'abominations' of Proverbs 6:16.

In verse 9 the BSB's footnote offers 'flattery' for the phrase translated 'deceit.' The underlying verb belongs to a root for smoothness, the speech that slides easily and slips past a listener's guard. That fits the throat that is an open grave: pleasant on top, deadly beneath. Paul quotes the line in Romans 3:13 from the Greek psalter.

The word rendered 'my enemies' in verse 8 comes from a root for watching. It names those who lie in wait and observe. The same word appears in Psalm 27:11 in the very same phrase, 'because of my oppressors,' and there too it sits beside the request to be led on a level path. The two psalms share a pair: a road to walk and watchers on it.

In verse 7 'I will bow down' translates a Hebrew verb that means to prostrate the body, the same word used of worship at Shiloh, 1 Samuel 1:3. And the 'shield' of verse 12 is a tsinnah, the large body shield carried before a soldier, 1 Samuel 17:7, not the small round shield. God's favor is pictured as covering the whole person.

The prayer of verse 10, 'declare them guilty,' rests on the Hebrew word for guilt, asham, in a form that means to treat someone as culpable or make them bear their guilt. It is a courtroom request, addressed to the Judge, and not a curse spoken at the enemy. The phrase 'by their own devices' is literally by their own counsels, so the plots they laid become the ground on which they fall.

typology.type: The morning lamb and the laid out prayer, Psalm 5:3
typology.fulfillment: Israel began each day with a lamb on the altar, Exodus 29:38-42, and David's prayer is arranged like that offering. The correspondence points ahead to Christ, 'the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world,' John 1:29, whose one offering makes the daily repetition unnecessary, Hebrews 10:11-14. The type falls short in that the morning lamb could not cleanse a conscience, and David still had to return to the altar the next day. In Christ the offering is finished, and the morning becomes an occasion for gratitude, not for renewed payment.

typology.type: Entering God's house by loving devotion, Psalm 5:7
typology.fulfillment: David crosses the threshold on the strength of God's chesed and not his own record. The pattern is completed when believers enter 'the Most Holy Place by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way opened for us through the curtain of His body,' Hebrews 10:19-20. Jesus is also the temple itself, John 2:19-21, and the way to the Father, John 14:6. The type is surpassed because David bowed toward a building, while the church enters the presence of God in a person, and one day in a city with no temple, Revelation 21:22.

typology.type: The righteous sufferer among lying witnesses, Psalm 5:9
typology.fulfillment: David faces mouths in which there is nothing steady or true. The pattern comes to a head at Jesus' trial, where 'many bore false witness against Jesus, but their testimony was inconsistent,' Mark 14:56. The escalation is that David asks God to expose the liars, while Jesus prays for the men who nailed Him up, Luke 23:34, and bears their guilt, 2 Corinthians 5:21. The type falls short because David was not sinless, whereas Christ is the truly righteous one whose innocence the accusers could not disprove.

typology.type: Those who take refuge and rejoice, Psalm 5:11
typology.fulfillment: The circle of those who 'love Your name' and shout for joy prefigures the people who have not seen Christ and yet 'love' and 'rejoice with an inexpressible and glorious joy,' 1 Peter 1:8. David's refuge is the LORD's shelter and shield; the New Testament fills it with a person, for those in Christ are kept in the Father's hand, John 10:28-29. The correspondence is real, but the psalm sings of joy in hope of deliverance, while the New Testament sings of joy already given in the risen Lord.

study.christ:
The psalm leads to Christ first by the pattern of the righteous one under false witness. David complains that not a word from his enemies can be trusted, and the Gospels say almost the same thing about Jesus' trial, where the chief priests looked for testimony and could not make the accounts agree, Mark 14:55-59. Jesus did not answer slander with slander. The psalm's cry for God to act is heard in the quiet way that God vindicated His Son, by raising Him.

It leads to Christ by the image of the open grave. David's enemies are throats that swallow, tombs that give off the smell of death. Jesus uses tomb language of the religious leaders of His day, calling them 'whitewashed tombs,' Matthew 23:27, and Paul applies David's line to the whole human race in Romans 3:13. Yet the tomb outside Jerusalem tells the other half of the story: the grave that seemed to be the end was opened from the inside, and it was the grave of the only man who never spoke a false word. The pattern is not an allegory of every detail, but the contrast is true: humanity's mouth is a grave, and Christ came out of one.

It leads to Christ by the doorway of verse 7. David enters God's house 'by the abundance of Your loving devotion.' John's Gospel says that Jesus came 'full of grace and truth,' John 1:14, the New Testament pair that matches the Old Testament chesed and faithfulness, and that 'from His fullness we have all received grace upon grace,' John 1:16. What David could only ask for, the church has received in a person. That same person is the temple, John 2:19-21, the way, John 14:6, and the curtain through which we pass, Hebrews 10:20.

It leads to Christ by the request 'Lead me, O LORD, in Your righteousness.' The gospel tells us that God's righteousness has been shown in Christ, Romans 3:21-22, and that Christ 'has become for us wisdom from God: our righteousness, holiness, and redemption,' 1 Corinthians 1:30. David asks to be guided along a righteousness that is not his own, and the answer is a Savior who walks ahead on that road.

Finally, the prayer 'declare them guilty' finds its counterpart in Christ's role as Judge, John 5:22, and in the wonder that God 'made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf,' 2 Corinthians 5:21. The guilt that David wants declared on the wicked was, at the cross, declared on a substitute so that the wicked might be pardoned. We should not force every line of the psalm into the life of Jesus. But this prayer, which rests entirely on mercy and appeals to God's justice, was answered in Him at both points.
study.god:
This psalm gives an unusual picture of God because it describes Him almost entirely by what He will not do. He does not delight in wickedness. Evil cannot stay with Him as a guest. The boastful cannot stand before Him. The negatives are not the mood of an irritable deity; they show that His goodness is so real that anything opposed to it is out of place in His presence. Holiness is not a mood but the settled character of the One who is life and light, and the psalm treats it that way.

He is a King who hears, verse 2. David calls Him 'my King and my God' before any request is made, so the appeal is not to an official who might be persuaded but to a ruler whose ear is already turned. Psalm 84:3 uses the same address for a God who gives even the sparrow a home. And He is a King who acts in the morning, when justice was done in Israel's gates, Zephaniah 3:5. He is not slow or absent.

He has feelings of a moral kind. The psalm says He delights, hates, abhors and blesses. Scripture does not treat these as the outbursts of a temper but as the steady response of a perfect person to good and evil. The same God who 'hates' the lover of violence, Psalm 11:5, is the One who guards those who take refuge and surrounds them with favor.

The greatest tension in the psalm is the one between His holiness and His welcome. Verse 4 shuts the door and verse 7 opens it. The two are not solved by softening either one. God does not lower His standard so that David can enter; He supplies a way, loving devotion, that honors both His holiness and His mercy. The rest of the Bible tells how He did so, in the blood of Jesus, Hebrews 10:19.

He is also a guide. 'Lead me' and 'make straight Your way before me' show that God is not only Judge of the past but Companion for the road, and that He cares about the roads His people take because of those who lie in wait.

For worship, the psalm teaches reverence first, 'in reverence I will bow down,' verse 7, and then joy, 'let them ever shout for joy,' verse 11. We are to come with awe because He is holy and with gladness because He has opened His house. The final verse tells us what to remember when the day is done: He blesses the righteous, and He does so with a shield that covers the whole person.

crossReferences.note: The question 'who may abide in Your tent' uses the same guest language as 'no evil can dwell with You' in Psalm 5:4. Psalm 15 answers with a portrait of integrity, while Psalm 5 answers with mercy. Read together, they hold the standard and the gift side by side.

David asks to be led on a level path 'because of my oppressors' and names 'false witnesses' who breathe out violence. The wording of Psalm 27:11 matches Psalm 5:8, and the lying accusers of Psalm 5:9 reappear. The two prayers belong to the same kind of season.

The Psalter's second psalm ends by blessing all who take refuge in the Son. Psalm 5:11 picks up that word and asks that those who take refuge be sheltered. Refuge is the door by which anyone enters the blessing the first psalms describe.

The daily morning lamb, offered at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting where God promised to meet His people. Psalm 5:3 is prayed at the same hour. The psalm shows the inward meaning of the ritual, a person coming with expectation to the place where God speaks.

'He applies His justice morning by morning; He does not fail at dawn.' This gives a reason why David prays at daybreak. Morning was when righteous judgment was expected, so he brings his case when God's court sits.

Paul builds a chain of Old Testament lines to show that all are under sin, and 'Their throats are open graves' comes from Psalm 5:9. David's portrait of his enemies becomes a portrait of humanity, so the prayer must be prayed with a personal 'and me too.'

Believers have 'confidence to enter the Most Holy Place by the blood of Jesus.' What Psalm 5:7 hoped for, entry by loving devotion, is opened by Christ's body. The result is that we can draw near 'in full assurance of faith' without fear of being shut out.

At Jesus' trial many bore false witness and their testimony was inconsistent. The slanderers whose words 'cannot be trusted' in Psalm 5:9 find their fullest example here, in the trial of the one man who was truly innocent.

Solomon asks that God's eyes be open toward the temple so that He will hear prayer offered toward that place. David's bowing 'toward Your holy temple' belongs to the same practice, and it shows that Israel prayed toward the place of God's name.

'His mercies never fail. They are new every morning.' This is the promise behind David's morning prayer. The chesed of Psalm 5:7 is not used up; it is renewed each day, which is why he can come again at daybreak.

Jesus goes out 'early in the morning, while it was still dark' to a solitary place to pray. It is the New Testament image of the habit Psalm 5:3 describes, and it shows that the Son of God did not think Himself above the pattern of dawn prayer.

study.oneStory:
The psalm's opening question, who can come near a holy God, is older than David. It begins in Eden, where the man and the woman heard the LORD God walking in the garden and hid, Genesis 3:8, and were then barred by cherubim from the way to the tree of life, Genesis 3:24. Psalm 5:4 is the sober summary of that expulsion: evil cannot stay with God. The story of Scripture has to explain how anyone could return.

The answer is built up in stages. At Sinai the LORD set a tent among His people, with a daily lamb, an altar, and a veil, Exodus 29:38-42. The temple in Jerusalem raised that answer in stone, and the prayers of Israel were offered toward it, 1 Kings 8:29-30. Psalm 5 is the voice of a person who lives inside that system and knows what the system means. Its rules, its lamb and its curtain teach that entry is possible only by God's provision. David's 'abundance of Your loving devotion' is not a rejection of the system but its inner truth.

Then the psalm meets the darkness of the fall in the character of David's enemies. Their mouths are open graves, and Paul takes that to mean the whole human family, Romans 3:13. This is the fallen world in a single image: speech that ought to bless is used to kill. The rest of the Bible is the story of the Word who came from God's mouth and did not deceive.

The story turns in Christ. He is the true temple, the way in, the lamb and the priest. Through Him, those who take refuge are shielded, and they enter God's presence with confidence, Hebrews 10:19-22. The church lives in an age when the morning of the new creation has broken, Luke 24:1, but the enemies of the psalm are not yet gone.

It ends where the psalm points. In the new creation the gates of the city 'will never be shut at the end of the day, because there will be no night there,' Revelation 21:25, and 'nothing unclean will ever enter it, nor anyone who practices an abomination or a lie,' Revelation 21:27. The liars of Psalm 5 are outside, and the faithful come in, not by their own righteousness but because their names are 'written in the Lamb's Book of Life.' God's servants will worship Him and 'see His face,' Revelation 22:3-4. The prayer that began at daybreak with a watchman's hope finds its answer in a day that never ends.

quiz.q: What does David ask God to do at the start of Psalm 5?

options.text: Give ear to his words, consider his groaning, and attend to his cry, since he lays his plea before God every morning.
options.note: This is the psalm's opening morning petition.

options.text: Reveal the identity of his enemies to him.
options.note: David is aware of deceitful enemies already; his opening plea is simply for God to hear him, not to reveal identities.

options.text: Grant him victory in an upcoming battle.
options.note: The psalm's opening concern is being heard in prayer, not a specific battle.

options.text: Nothing; the psalm opens in silence.
options.note: Verses 1-3 are an urgent, explicit plea to be heard.

quiz.q: What does Psalm 5:4-6 reveal about God's character?

options.text: He does not delight in wickedness, and no evil, boasting, or deceit can dwell in His presence.
options.note: This section describes God's holiness in relation to evil directly and repeatedly.

options.text: He is indifferent to human sin.
options.note: The passage shows the opposite, God actively opposed to evil, not indifferent.

options.text: He delights equally in good and evil.
options.note: The text explicitly states God does not delight in wickedness; there is no equal delight in evil.

options.text: He has no moral character at all.
options.note: This section is precisely about God's clear, holy moral character.

quiz.q: On what basis does David say he will enter God's house in verse 7?

options.text: By the abundance of God's loving devotion, not his own merit.
options.note: This is the psalm's central statement about access to God's presence.

options.text: By his own perfect righteousness.
options.note: David explicitly credits access to God's mercy, chesed, not his own righteousness.

options.text: By offering a large sacrifice.
options.note: The verse specifically names God's abundant loving devotion as the basis, not a specific sacrifice.

options.text: By his royal status as king.
options.note: The verse gives no basis in royal status; it credits God's mercy alone.

quiz.q: How does the psalm describe the speech of the enemies in verse 9?

options.text: Not a word can be trusted; their throats are open graves and their tongues practice deceit.
options.note: Paul quotes this very image in Romans 3:13 to describe universal human sinfulness.

options.text: They speak truthfully but act wickedly.
options.note: The verse specifically targets their speech itself as untrustworthy, not merely a mismatch between words and actions.

options.text: They rarely speak at all.
options.note: The verse describes active, deceitful speech, not silence.

options.text: Their words are mostly harmless exaggeration.
options.note: The image of an open grave describes deadly, destructive speech, far beyond harmless exaggeration.

quiz.q: What is promised to those who take refuge in the LORD in verses 11-12?

options.text: Joy, shelter, and God's favor surrounding them like a shield.
options.note: The psalm closes with this triple promise for those who trust in God.

options.text: Freedom from all future hardship.
options.note: The psalm promises God's favor and shelter, not a guarantee against all future hardship.

options.text: Wealth and social status.
options.note: The promise is joy and divine shelter, not material wealth or status.

options.text: Nothing; the psalm ends without any promise.
options.note: Verses 11-12 explicitly promise joy, shelter, and God's favor.

questions: David brings his morning prayer to God before facing the day's enemies and challenges. What would it look like for you to lay your plea before God at the start of your day rather than as an afterthought?

David is confident he can only enter God's house by the abundance of God's loving devotion, not his own merit. Where are you tempted to think your standing with God depends on your own performance rather than His mercy?

The psalm names the specific danger of deceitful speech, words that destroy like an open grave. Where might careless or deceptive words, yours or others', be doing quiet damage in your relationships right now?
David asks God to deal justly with his enemies rather than taking revenge himself. Is there a situation where you need to release your desire for personal vengeance and trust God's justice instead?

The psalm ends in joy for those who take refuge in the LORD, sheltered like something surrounded by a shield. Where do you need to actively take refuge in God this week rather than trying to shield yourself?

translationNotes.note: Lay my plea before You can also be rendered order my prayer, using an image of arranging a sacrifice on an altar, suggesting careful, deliberate morning prayer rather than a hurried request.
By the abundance of Your loving devotion translates berov chasdecha, grounding all access to God's house in His covenant chesed rather than any human merit or ritual qualification.
Their throats are open graves is quoted by Paul in Romans 3:13 as part of his composite Old Testament indictment of universal human sinfulness in Romans 3:10-18.
